lines.text: Two thirty-one in the morning. Day eight.
The alarm in aisle twelve is ringing again.
And every dead thing outside Freshway can hear it.
You turn it off. And under the clock, there's a candy wrapper.
Sour worms. Still sticky.
Kid. That wasn't me.
Two people are locked inside this store. One of them is lying.
And in three days, you run out of water.
This week, you'll cross to the mall. You'll meet someone alive.
And you'll learn what Dale has been hiding.
Day eight. Here's the new map of Freshway.
The front is yours. Fourteen aisles. Eight thousand cans. Gary's office.
The back is Dale's. The stockroom. The freezer. And the wall you built out of bottled water.
Every gallon you have is in that wall. And Dale is on the other side of it.
On day seven, he jammed the stockroom doors shut.
Here's how this works, kid. You stay up front. I stay in back. Nobody gets hurt.
And the water?
One gallon. For twenty cans. Every morning.
Twenty cans for one gallon. In a normal store, that's a terrible deal. This is not a normal store anymore.
So how many cans you got left, anyway?
He wants to know how many cans you have.
Rule four. Never tell anyone what you have.
Maybe a hundred.
Last week you said nine thousand.
It's been a long week.
You have eight thousand nine hundred.
At twenty cans a day, that's enough to buy water for over a year. As long as Dale keeps his word.
Day nine. Seven in the morning. The gallon doesn't come.
Tell me the real number, kid. Then the water comes back.
Problem one. Water.
A person needs about three liters a day. With none, you get about three days.
So you need water Dale doesn't control. Today.
You try the faucet in the staff restroom.
It coughs. Spits. And stops.
City water runs on pumps. No power, no pumps. The towers drain in a day or two.
But every building with hot water keeps a tank of it.
This one holds twenty gallons. Clean. And it's on your side of the border.
There's a drain valve at the bottom. The first gallon comes out brown. Then it runs clear.
Water that sits in a tank can grow things. So before you drink it, you clean it.
Eight drops of plain bleach per gallon. Then wait thirty minutes.
Aisle four has bleach. Gary labeled the shelf, of course.
And the toilet tanks. Not the bowls. The tanks. Same water as the tap.
Twenty gallons, plus four tanks. If you're careful, that's about a month.
Problem one. Solved.
That night, the radio clicks.
Heard you found the water heater. Smart.
Guess you don't need my water anymore.
You never told him.
Then you hear it. A tap. In the pipes.
The pipes run through the whole building. Every sound in that restroom ends up in his ear.
Rule five. The walls have ears.
Later that night, the pipes carry something else.
Dale's voice. Not on the radio. Through the wall.
Ninety-eight. Ninety-nine. A hundred. Ready or not.
He's counting. Like a kid playing hide-and-seek.
Who counts to a hundred in an empty store?
Eleven at night. You climb to the roof.
The light in the mall is still on. Top floor. Same window.
Last week, you decided nobody was over there.
And then it blinks.
Three short. Three long. Three short.
S. O. S. Somebody over there is alive. And asking for help.
Not on the radio. With a lamp. Whoever it is, they don't want Dale to hear.
Would you go? Tell me in the comments.
Day ten. The decoy clocks are gone. And Dale knows that trick anyway.
You need a sound bigger than you. Bigger than anything.
Then, at two in the afternoon, the sky goes dark.
A storm is coming.
Heavy rain is about fifty decibels. Footsteps on wet asphalt, about thirty.
In a storm, they can't pick you out. They just stand there. Listening to the sky.
And the thunder tells you where the storm is.
Count from the flash to the boom. Every three seconds is about a kilometer.
Flash. One. Two. Boom. Less than a kilometer.
When the flash and the boom come together, it's right on top of you. That's the loudest it gets.
You pack light. A flashlight. A hammer from aisle three. And the radio, turned all the way down.
Before you go, you chain the stockroom doors. From your side.
Going somewhere, kid?
Rule four. You don't answer.
Two hundred of them. Standing in the rain. Faces up.
Nobody turns.
Halfway across, your shoe hits a bottle.
It clinks against a car. The closest one is two steps away.
The rain eats the sound. You keep walking.
The mall's side door is chained. The glass next to it isn't.
Flash. One. Boom. Close. Not close enough.
You wait. Rain on your neck. Hammer in your hand.
Flash and boom, together. You swing.
Brookfield Mall. Four floors. Dark.
Rain drums on the glass roof. It's the loudest room you've ever stood in. Good.
Around the dry fountain, thirty of them.
Shoppers. A security guard. A kid from the pretzel stand, still in his paper hat.
They were shopping when it started. Some of them are still holding the bags.
The window was on the top floor. The escalators stopped when the power did.
A stopped escalator is just stairs. Loud stairs. Metal.
You walk on the edges. Where the steps are bolted down.
Level two. A toy store. Every teddy bear still in the window.
Level three. The cinema. The poster still says coming soon.
Top floor. A store called Bright Tech. The lantern is in the window.
Nobody's there.
A sleeping bag. Two backpacks. A solar panel taped to the glass.
And a desk lamp, wired to the panel. That's the light you've been watching all week.
Then something cold touches the back of your neck.
Don't. Move.
It's a fire extinguisher. Held by a girl. Fifteen. Maybe.
You're the Freshway guy.
She knows you.
I've been listening to you. Every night. Channel three.
Then why didn't you say something?
My button's broken. I can hear. I can't talk.
So she used the light. And a page of Morse code from the bookstore on level two.
Rule three. Count the radios. There are three.
Rate your day, one to ten. Every single night.
She does a pretty good Dale.
The storm ends at six. And the silence comes back.
You're not crossing that lot tonight.
Her name is Nora. She's been here since the first night.
My mom worked nights here. Inventory.
She doesn't say what happened to her mom. You don't ask.
My little brother went across the street that night. To Freshway. For candy.
He's nine. His name is Leo.
You were in Freshway that night. You never saw a kid.
Every night, at two thirty-one, there's an alarm over there. I can hear it from here.
That's him. That's how I know he's alive.
You think about the batteries. Somebody keeps putting new ones in that clock.
The candy wrapper. Sour worms.
Somebody small. Who likes sour worms.
Then Nora's radio clicks. Not channel three. Channel four.
Nora? Honey? Are you there?
Nora goes white.
That's my dad.
Dale is her father.
Channel four is ours. He calls every night. And I can't answer.
Mall security. That part was true. He just wasn't at the mall.
He asked how many of you there were. He asked about the freezer. He asked about the alarm.
He wasn't counting your food. He was looking for his son.
Rule four works both ways. Dale never told you what he has.
He has a son. Somewhere inside Freshway.
And now you know where his daughter is.
Take me back with you. Please.
Day twelve. The lot fills up again. You wait for a plan.
Nora has rules too. She wrote them on the back of a receipt.
Never sleep on the ground floor. Shoes off on the escalator. And the sour worms are for Leo.
She's been saving one bag for twelve days.
At two thirty-one, the alarm rings across the street.
Faint. Like a phone ringing in another room.
Hi, Leo.
She says it every night.
Day thirteen. One in the morning. Time to go home. Both of you.
No storm. No clocks. Just two hundred of them in the lot.
Nora has an idea. Bright Tech sells drones.
And a speaker that clips onto anything.
Every time you double the distance, a sound gets about six decibels quieter.
So the song has to go far. And you have to stay very quiet.
Rule two. Music is a dinner bell. This time, you ring it on purpose.
The box says thirty minutes of flight. That's the plan's clock.
Nora has one song on her phone. Guess which one.
Two hundred dead people follow a song about discount yogurt. To the far end of the lot.
You go down the escalator. Shoes in your hands.
Out the side door. Past the broken glass. Into the lot.
Then the drone beeps. Low battery.
Twelve minutes early. Cheap drone.
The song stops. Two hundred heads turn back toward the store.
You run for the staff door. Gary's keys. The fourth one. You remember this time.
You're in. Both of you.
Day fourteen. Here's what you know.
Rule one. They hear. They don't see.
Rule two. Music is a dinner bell.
Rule three. Count the radios.
Rule four. Never tell anyone what you have.
Rule five. The walls have ears.
The radio clicks.
You brought her home. Thank you.
Where's Leo, Dad?
Dale doesn't answer. For a long time, the radio just hisses.
I've looked everywhere, honey. Every night. I count to a hundred. And I look.
It's his favorite game. He always hides. You always find him.
Two thirty-one.
The alarm in aisle twelve starts to ring.
Nora runs.
Next to the clock, there's a drawing. In crayon.
A girl. A man in a cap. And you. Orange headphones and all.
Under it, three words. Come find me.
Leo is alive. He's in this store. And they don't see you. But he does.
